label: bm-formlabs-all-resins
topic: Every Formlabs resin and powder, as a design space
summary: Fetched 2026-11-12 (UTC): the Formlabs materials catalogue, the solvent-compatibility table, the data-sheet index, 57 product pages, 54 English technical data sheets (TDS, PDF; 7 more are web-format TDS pages) and 18 safety data sheets (all saved with URL, date, byte size and sha256 in data/formlabs-tds/MANIFEST.tsv). The table has 48 rows: 23 current Form 4-family SLA resins (including casting, ceramic and colour bases), 7 Form 4B medical resins, 10 legacy or Form 3-only resins, and 8 powders (Nylon 12, 12 White, 12 Tough, 12 GF, 11, 11 CF, TPU 90A, and Polypropylene, which is no longer on the catalogue); Nylon 11 Pro and the six Alpha resins are in findings (web-format TDS). Per material: tensile and flexural modulus, UTS, elongation, Shore, HDT, density where published, 24 h cube water and IPA uptake, biocompatibility standards, minimum layer thickness, printers and the post-cure recipe from the TDS footnotes, state by state (green and post-cured). Main results. (1) Earlier agents are confirmed on the cube table (all current resins 0.0-0.9% water in 24 h; Elastic 50A V2 39.2% IPA vs Rigid 10K <0.1%) but one claim must be narrowed: Flexible 80A Resin V2 gains +8% mass and +3% volume in 1 day in water (+9%/+7% in 1 week) in its own TDS slab test, so "stock resins gain under 1%" is false for that resin, and the 0.7% quoted for Flexible 80A in the cube table is the V1 row. (2) The Grey V5 one-week water figures (+3.23% mass, modulus to 65%) are now read cleanly and confirmed. (3) Flexible 50A is the renamed Elastic 50A V2. (4) Chemistry: all Form 4 resins except Silicone 40A are methacrylate/urethane-methacrylate (SDS), so acrylate pairs can co-cure; Silicone 40A is polysiloxane with no bonding evidence. (5) Ranking: the best pairs are Flexible 80A V2 (active) with Rigid 10K, Rigid 4000, Tough 2000 V2, Grey/Clear V5 or Tough 1000 (passive); applying the project 3/2 law with the 0.2 mm wall limit, the printable curvature is best with soft partners (Flexible 50A 26.6 /m, Silicone 40A 20.1 /m at 1 day) because the optimum thickness ratio n^(-1/2) is impractical for stiff partners (8.3 mm of Flexible 80A V2 over 0.2 mm of Rigid 10K). (6) Gaps: no humid-air swelling, no diffusivity, no elastomer moduli, no measured adhesion, slab thickness of the 80A V2 test unstated. All swelling-based curvature numbers are own calculations with stated assumptions and should be replaced by coupon measurements.
lay_summary: Formlabs sells about sixty liquid resins and a handful of nylon powders for its 3D printers. We downloaded the official data sheets for all of them and lined up how stiff each one is and how much water or alcohol it soaks up. Almost all of them barely drink water, less than one percent of their weight in a day, so they would hardly change shape in humid air. One soft resin is the exception: it swells about three percent in volume after a day in water, which is enough to make a thin strip bend. Think of a strip of wet paper stuck to a strip of plastic: the paper swells, the plastic does not, and the pair curls. The best pairs are that soft resin glued to a stiff one from the same chemical family. Nobody has published how strongly two Formlabs materials stick to each other, or how fast humid air gets into them, so the next step is a small printed test strip, not more reading.

glossary.plain: a printer that hardens liquid resin layer by layer with a violet light
a printer that fuses nylon or rubber powder layer by layer with a laser
the maker's technical data sheet (properties) and safety data sheet (ingredients)
how stiff a material is: the force needed to stretch or bend it a little; bigger means stiffer
a rough stiffness taken as stress at a fixed stretch divided by that stretch; used here where no modulus is published
hardness scales from pressing a pin in; A for rubbers, D for hard plastics
heat deflection temperature: the temperature at which a loaded bar starts to sag
freshly printed and washed, versus after extra light and heat that finishes hardening it
taking up water or solvent so the part gets heavier and bigger
isopropyl alcohol, the liquid used to wash printed resin parts
two thin layers of different materials bonded together; if one swells it bends the pair
how tightly a strip bends, in 1/metre; 20 per metre means a circle of radius 5 cm
the two chemical families here: plastic-like acrylics that cure together, versus silicone, which sticks poorly to other things
a paid Formlabs setting that lets the printer run non-Formlabs resin or powder
a simple model of how rubber stretches, used to correct the rough stiffness estimate

key_claims.claim: Flexible 80A Resin V2 gains +8% mass and +3% volume in 1 day in deionized water and +9% / +7% in 1 week (ASTM D471 slabs); it is the only current Formlabs resin with swelling large enough to drive a hygromorph, and it contradicts a blanket "under 1% in 24 h" for stock resins.

Every other Form 4-family resin gains 0.0-0.9% mass in water in Formlabs own 24 h 1 cm cube test (Clear V5 0.9, Tough 1000 0.0, Rigid 10K <0.1); no humid-air swelling or diffusivity exists for any of them.
Elastic/Flexible 50A takes 39.2% IPA in 24 h against under 0.1% for Rigid 10K (earlier finding confirmed): the largest solvent-swelling contrast between two Form 4 resins of the same chemistry.

All Form 4 SLA resins except Silicone 40A are (meth)acrylate photopolymers per their SDS (co-curable, so bilayer bonding is plausible); Silicone 40A is polysiloxane and no source supports its bonding to acrylates. No measured bond strength between any two Formlabs materials exists in the sources read.

recommendations: Print a coupon set before any design work: Flexible 80A V2 strips (0.2, 0.5, 1 mm) bonded or co-printed to Tough 1000, Flexible 50A, Silicone 40A and Rigid 10K, soaked in water at 23 C and in 60/90% RH air; weigh and measure length and curvature at 1, 6, 24, 168 h. This replaces every estimated number in this report.
Ask Formlabs (or test) the slab thickness behind the +8%/+3% result and run the same slab test on Flexible 50A, Tough 1000 and Rigid 10K so that swelling contrast is measured on one method.
Treat Silicone 40A as a high-risk partner: run a peel test of Flexible 80A V2 or Tough 1000 cured against cured Silicone 40A before committing.
Fuse route: no co-printing; if a powder bilayer is wanted, bond Nylon 11 and TPU 90A with an adhesive and test it; Nylon 11 is the only bio-based claim, ask Formlabs for the percentage.

Beyond stock resins (Open Material Mode): the earlier agent found PEG-acrylate hydrogel resins swell 3.5-74% linearly (Maennel 2020, DLP printer, not Formlabs); that is the route to a much larger curvature; not re-examined here.
Keep the IPA wash step in mind: elastomer bilayers will curl in it; design the wash time and fixture accordingly.
